Saya sebentar tadi 3 jam bersama Yb Datuk Seri Dr Zaliha di kediamannya. Kami bicara dgn pandangan masing2. Berdasarkan pandangan dan data.

Dr Zaliha yakin PH boleh lakukan kejutan. Saya juga beritahu perkara yg sama… tidak sepertimana di Sabah kita tahu kita akn kalah sebelum bertanding. Kali ini kita yakin boleh lakukan kejutan atau lebih baik dari keputusan sebelum ini.

Cerita isu di N9, saya pelik kenapa berlaku ia berlaku. Saya tidak mahu campur urusan adat.. tapi terfikir juga adakah semudah itu utk gugurkan seorang Raja dari takhtanya. Mesti kena ada sebabnya bukan?

Sehingga ini, DYMM Tuanku Muhriz Masih Kekal Yang DiPertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan

Jika mahu dikosongkan, atas sebab apa? Harus ada sebab/alasan kukuh beserta INQUIRY, yang ada prosesnya dan perlu disaksikan dan dicop oleh Menteri Besar.

Persoalannya sekarang, Tuanku Muhriz masih lagi sihat walafiat, tapi mengapa ada gerakan untuk Pemahsyuran YamTuan Baharu? Ini antara topik yg dibangkitkan rakan2.

Surat ini sebenarnya memberi petunjuk yang sangat menarik tentang tafsiran Perlembagaan Negeri Sembilan.

Peguam yang mewakili "Undang Yang Empat dan Tengku Besar Tampin" berhujah bahawa pembubaran DUN melanggar:

Fasal 56(2) → kuasa pembubaran DUN.

Fasal 38(4) → berkaitan pelantikan dan kedudukan EXCO.

Fasal 28(1) & (2) → definisi dan pelaksanaan kuasa "Ruler". 

Ini konsisten dengan satu hujah perlembagaan yang memang boleh dibina daripada teks Perlembagaan Negeri Sembilan.

Hujah mereka nampaknya begini

Fasal 56(2) kata:

> "The Ruler may prorogue or dissolve the Legislative Assembly." 

Tetapi Fasal 28(1) pula kata:

> Dalam Bahagian Kedua Perlembagaan, "Ruler" bermaksud Yang di-Pertuan Besar dan Ruling Chiefs (Undang yang memegang jawatan dan ada pada masa itu). 

Oleh sebab Fasal 56 berada dalam Bahagian Kedua, mereka berhujah bahawa:

> Pembubaran DUN bukan tindakan YDPB seorang diri, tetapi tindakan "Ruler" mengikut definisi Fasal 28.

Itulah sebab surat ini menyebut bahawa tiada persetujuan diperoleh daripada anak guam mereka.
---
Tetapi ada juga hujah balas

Pihak yang mempertahankan pembubaran boleh berhujah:

1. Amalan perlembagaan selama ini ialah pembubaran dibuat melalui YDPB.

2. Fasal 40(2)(b) memberi budi bicara kepada YDPB mengenai pembubaran DUN. 

3. Fasal 28 tidak semestinya bermaksud semua tindakan "Ruler" memerlukan persetujuan aktif setiap Undang.
---
Apa yang menarik?

Saya dapati surat ini tidak bergantung kepada Fasal 10 (pelucutan takhta). Sebaliknya, mereka bergantung kepada:

> Fasal 28 + Fasal 56

iaitu hujah bahawa "Ruler" dalam Negeri Sembilan bukan semata-mata YDPB tetapi satu institusi yang turut melibatkan Undang. 

Jujurnya, daripada teks Perlembagaan yang kita baca, ini bukan hujah remeh. Ia mempunyai asas literal yang agak kuat kerana Fasal 28 memang mentakrifkan "Ruler" secara berbeza daripada negeri-negeri lain. 

Persoalan yang akan menentukan siapa betul ialah:

> Adakah Fasal 28 menyebabkan persetujuan Undang menjadi syarat sah pembubaran DUN, atau adakah kuasa budi bicara YDPB dalam Fasal 40(2)(b) mengatasi tafsiran tersebut?

Itulah titik pertikaian sebenar yang nampak daripada surat ini.

Jam 11.05am ada court injunction menghalang “pemasyhuran”. Maksud siri perlantikan ini episod masih panjang.

Maklumat yg saya terima rakyat N9 berang dgn tindakan UMNO yg seolah olah campur tangan dlm isu Istana ini. Ini pandangan rakan dan saudara saya di N9.

Perintah sementara mahkamah itu menghalang plaintif sama ada secara langsung atau melalui wakil mereka daripada memanggil atau mengadakan sebarang mesyuarat DKU termasuk Sidang Khas yang dijadual berlangsung hari ini.

Ini cerita N9 yg dimaklumkan rakan2 mengenai perkembangan semasa. So kita tunggu sahaja. Politik org Melayu sgt luar biasa tidak pernah aman dgn projek tebuk atap.

Text:
Kesahihan pelantikan Yang di-Pertuan Besar (YDPB) yang baharu diisytiharkan hari ini, Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja'afar, kini dipertikaikan sepenuhnya dan berada dalam keadaan tergantung susulan perintah mahkamah serta pendirian rasmi kerajaan. 
Berikut adalah fakta undang-undang dan situasi semasa berhubung krisis ini:
Status Perintah Mahkamah (Status Quo)
Injunksi Sementara Dikeluarkan: Mahkamah Tinggi Seremban yang dipimpin oleh Hakim Roz Mawar Rozain telah mengeluarkan perintah injunksi ad interim (sementara) untuk mengekalkan status quo pentadbiran Dewan Keadilan dan Undang Negeri Sembilan (DKU). 
Sidang Khas Dihalang: Perintah ini secara khusus melarang sebarang mesyuarat, termasuk Sidang Khas DKU yang sepatutnya berlangsung hari ini, daripada membuat sebarang keputusan atau tindakan pentadbiran. 
Sekatan Undang-Undang: Peguam kanan, Steven Thiru, mengesahkan bahawa larangan tersebut merangkumi sebarang pelantikan baharu serta campur tangan dalam urusan pentadbiran DKU sehingga isu bidang kuasa diputuskan oleh mahkamah. Oleh itu, majlis pemasyhuran Tunku Nadzaruddin oleh Undang Yang Empat yang dilakukan di sebuah hotel di Melaka didakwa melanggar perintah pengekalan status quo ini. 
Pengiktirafan Kerajaan Persekutuan
Kerajaan Kekal Iktiraf Tuanku Muhriz: Perdana Menteri, Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, menegaskan bahawa Kerajaan Persekutuan kekal mengiktiraf Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir sebagai Yang di-Pertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan yang sah.
Tindakan Di Luar Saluran Sah: Perdana Menteri menyatakan bahawa sebarang pertikaian atau pengisytiharan takhta mestilah melalui saluran undang-undang dan Perlembagaan negeri yang betul bagi mengelakkan ketidakamanan.
Kesimpulannya, pelantikan YDPB baharu hari ini tidak diiktiraf oleh kerajaan dan dianggap tidak sah di bawah perintah status quo yang dikeluarkan oleh Mahkamah Tinggi Seremban sehingga kes penuh selesai dibicarakan.

Text:
Ini bermakna apa-apa pertabalan atau perlantikan adalah tidak sah?

***
Mahkamah Tinggi Seremban memberikan perintah injunksi sementara untuk mengekalkan status quo di tengah-tengah krisis diraja di Negeri Sembilan.

Hakim Roz Mawar Rozain memberikan injunksi sementara yang dimohon oleh dua defendan pertama, iaitu Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) serta setiausaha DKU Raja Norazli Raja Nordin.

Injunksi tersebut, yang bertujuan untuk mengekalkan status quo sehingga mahkamah dapat mendengar dan memutuskan perkara tersebut, mengenakan sekatan ke atas plaintif - empat Undang bersama-sama Tunku Besar Tampin dan Datuk Syahbandar Sungai Ujong.

Khususnya, plaintif, sama ada bertindak sendiri atau melalui wakil, telah dihalang daripada mengadakan mesyuarat, termasuk mesyuarat yang dijadualkan berlangsung hari ini, menjadikan sebarang keputusan mengenai urusannya, atau mengambil sebarang langkah yang mengganggu status quo majlis seperti yang berlaku sebelum 21 Mei.

Plaintif juga telah diperintahkan untuk tidak menggantung, melucutkan jawatan, atau mengganggu tugas Raja Norazli sebagai setiausaha DKU.

Perintah itu dikeluarkan selepas empat Undang menggantung perkhidmatan Raja Norazli pada 29 Mei, susulan dakwaan kegagalan pegawai tersebut mematuhi arahan terdahulu untuk mengadakan sidang khas pada hari tersebut bagi membincangkan pertikaian diraja negeri yang semakin buruk.
Dalam satu kenyataan hari ini, peguam Steven Thiru, yang mewakili DKU dan Raja Norazli, berkata perintah itu masih berkuat kuasa sementara menunggu pendengaran isu bidang kuasa mahkamah dan kewajaran, serta perintah mahkamah selanjutnya.

Dua defendan pertama juga diwakili oleh David Dinesh Mathew, Shafrin Halim, Gregory Das, dan Gurjeevan Singh.

Penasihat undang-undang negeri Muzalmah Mustapha Kamal dan Aala’uddin Baharom mewakili kerajaan Negeri Sembilan sebagai defendan ketiga.

Plaintif diwakili oleh Awang Armadajaya, Rhiza Ghazi, dan Asmawi Ismail.

Pada 14 Mei, Steven mempersoalkan kuasa Mahkamah Tinggi Seremban untuk mendengar kes tersebut, dengan alasan bahawa mahkamah tidak mempunyai bidang kuasa untuk mendengar saman pemula kerana DKU merupakan pihak berkuasa tertinggi untuk mentadbir adat Melayu di Negeri Sembilan.

Dia memetik Perkara 16(3) perlembagaan Negeri Sembilan, yang menetapkan bahawa nasihat DKU berkaitan adat Melayu di negeri ini tidak boleh dicabar di mahkamah atas apa jua alasan, termasuk mengenai penggantian atau penyingkiran mana-mana Undang.
Plaintif pada 5 Mei telah memfailkan saman pemula di mahkamah yang memohon untuk memaksa kerajaan negeri dan DKU mengeluarkan minit mesyuarat pada 17 April.

Ini berkaitan dengan sidang khas majlis tersebut, di mana keputusan dikatakan dicapai sebulat suara untuk meluluskan pemecatan Undang Sungai Ujong, Mubarak Thahak.

Sidang pada 17 April menjadi tumpuan kepada pertikaian diraja yang sedang berlangsung, yang menyaksikan tindakan balas Undang dengan pemecatan Yang di-Pertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir bulan lalu.

Text:
OPINION | Must a Negeri Sembilan Ruler Commit a Crime Before He Can Be Removed?

Zaid Ibrahim, the former law minister, recently gave an opinion about the Negeri Sembilan royal crisis that is similar to what a number of people, even those who comment on relevant posts in this page, have given.

According to Zaid, the purported “removal” of Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan by the Undang Yang Empat was inappropriate, because no clear misconduct was ever put before the public to justify the move.

“But we, the public, have not been told what wrongdoing Tuanku Muhriz supposedly committed. We simply do not know,” he said on his podcast.

According to Zaid, the central question was not merely whether the Undangs have the power to appoint or remove a ruler, but whether that power is exercised fairly and reasonably.

“Therefore, even if the four Undangs have the constitutional power to remove Tuanku Muhriz, I do not think it is appropriate. It is disproportionate.

“I believe the spirit of the constitutional provisions has been set aside. Even if the power to remove him exists, I do not think it should have been exercised in this manner,” Zaid added.

Personally, I must say that as a member of the public, I don't see the matter as how Zaid sees it at all.

First of all, in my view, I don't think the opinion of the public matters in the removal of the Yang Di-Pertuan Besar, because the opinion of the public was never a sought  in installing the Yang Di-Pertuan Besar in the first place.

If the public had nothing to do with the Yamtuan Besar's “hiring”, then I don't see why our approval is required in the Yamtuan Besar's “firing”.

As for the view that the Yamtuan Besar should only be subjected to “removal” if he has clearly committed a misconduct—which I assume Zaid is defining as murder, theft, fraud, etc.—I don't see why this is the case at all.

I am sure people get fired from their jobs even if they didn't steal, cheat, or murder in this world. They will get fired simply because they are deemed unfit for the job.

If you are a soldier, for example, and you are a gentle person who can't even bring yourself to hurt a fly, I think that is grounds for firing you even if you didn't steal, cheat, or murder.

If you are a service personnel, but you can't help but deal with your company's clients in a very strange, harsh, and uncompromising manner, you will probably be removed from your job too, even if you didn't do anything criminal.

My point here is that you can be removed from a job if you are simply deemed unfit for the job.

As per what the public understands, the Yang Di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan was  removed by the Undang Yang Empat because the Undangs deemed the Yamtuan Besar to be unfit for the job, not because he had done anything against the law.

As to why they deemed the Yamtuan Besar to be unfit for the job, does it really matter? If the constitution empowers them to judge the fitness of the Yamtuan Besar, then you cannot say that them using their constitutionally allocated powers to be unjust or inappropriate, just because they didn't give a specific reason.

In every election, the people also decide on whether we want the Prime Minister to continue his job for another term, but we have never told the Prime Minister why we want him removed, even when we remove them. If we judge that the Prime Minister is unfit for the job, we will just vote him out, and the Prime Minister is supposed to realise by himself that we voted him out because he has lost our confidence.

In the same way, you can also say that the Yamtuan Besar was likely removed from his office because he had simply lost the confidence of the Undangs.

As for the reason why, well, the Undangs seem to have given some vague reasons as to why they believe the Yamtuan Besar is unfit for his position, and it supposedly has to do with the Yamtuan Besar's “misconduct” in regards to matters related to adat.

What does that mean, you ask?

Well, to me, it just means that the Undangs don't think the Yamtuan Besar was acting as how they feel the Yamtuan Besar is supposed to act.

What does that mean, you ask again?

Well, let's use Zaid himself as an example. Say Zaid hired a lawyer to run his firm, but later he finds out that that lawyer is always arguing with him over everything, speaks to him in a condescending tone, cuts him off before he finishes his sentence, and acts as if he is Zaid's superior, although Zaid doesn't think he is his superior. Is Zaid unjust and inappropriate for terminating  that lawyer on the grounds that the said lawyer was not “practising decorum”  or "acting in a rude manner" or behaving in way that is "unbecoming" of an educated person?

How will Zaid explain why he found the lawyer's tone of voice unacceptable or prove that the lawyer is condescending ?

Must Zaid prove that the lawyer stole, cheated the firm, or committed fraud before he can terminate the lawyer?

Of course not. Zaid can terminate him if, according to their agreement, he is empowered to terminate the lawyer if he finds the lawyer to be unfit for the job, even if the reason that he has is something vague like the said lawyer was "rude" or "disrespectful" or conducted himself in a way that is "unbecoming" of a lawyer.

In the same way, I don't think the Undangs need to give exact reasons as to why they wish to remove the Yang Di-Pertuan Besar.

If the constitution empowers them to do it, then it is within their right to do so, and there is nothing unjust or inappropriate about it.

By the way, I am not saying this because I agree with the Undangs or am against the current Yamtuan Besar.

I am just saying this in response to the view that not only Zaid, but many people seem to have, which is that you can only remove the Yamtuan Besar, or anyone for that matter, if it is clearly proven that they have committed some serious misconduct like theft, murder, or arson. If there is no clear reason, then the removal is unjust or inappropriate.

I am opposed to this view simply because this is not how I see how the world works.

To gain better context, let’s look at the history of the situation.

Why Tuanku Ja'afar was proclaimed as ruler in 1967?

When Tuanku Munawir first became the Ruler of Negeri Sembilan, he made his only son, Tuanku Muhriz as heir presumptive (Tunku Besar) in 1960. However, when Tuanku Munawir passed on, Tuanku Muhriz was not chosen to succeed his father. He was only 19 years old. It has been suggested that the then Prime Minister of Malaysia, Tunku Abdul Rahman, influenced the Undangs not to choose Tuanku Muhriz on account of his youth. Instead the council chose his half-uncle Tuanku Jaafar to be the next Ruler.

In 1967, His Royal Highness Tuanku Ja’afar Ibni Almarhum Tuanku Abdul Rahman, aged 44, was proclaimed as the tenth Ruler of Negeri Sembilan. The proclamation was made by the Dato’ Undang Luak Jelebu, Dato’ Abu Bakar bin Ma’amor who led the Undang Yang Empat (the Four Chiefs) at the Balairong Sri Istana Besar, Sri Menanti, Negeri Sembilan. The appointment was made following the demise of his elder brother Tuanku Munawir on 14 April 1967.

Before becoming the Ruler, Tuanku Ja'afar's diplomatic career began in 1957. His first appointment was as Charge d' Affaires in Embassy of Malaysia, Washington, D.C. He also served as Deputy High Commissioner at the High Commission of Malaysia, London. He was later appointed as the Malaysian Ambassador to Egypt and then as High Commissioner to Nigeria and Ghana.

He was about to leave for Japan to serve as the Malaysian Ambassador to that country but was recalled by the State Government of Negeri Sembilan following the demise of his half brother.

During his reign, Tuanku Ja'afar became the tenth Yang di-Pertuan Agong of Malaysia (1994 to 1999). When he passed away in December 2008, Tuanku Muhriz finally succeeded him, becoming the Ruler of Negeri Sembilan, a few weeks before his 61st birthday.

Text:
CLEARING THE FOG  ON  THE ROYAL  MESS IN NEGRI SEMBILAN

FIRSTLY… WHAT DO ￼ BOTH, THE  NEGRI SEMBILAN  STATE AND FEDERAL CONSTITUTIONS SAY SINCE WE PRACTISE A CONSTITUTIONAL MONARCHY SYSTEM?

6 JUNE 2026

https://m.malaysiakini.com/news/776746

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has expressed his support for an election in Negeri Sembilan amid a royal crisis plaguing the state, stressing that the rule of law and customary practices must be adhered to at all times.

Declaring that the federal government continues to uphold Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir’s position as the Yang di-Pertuan Besar, Anwar said that while he has no objections to the voicing of dissenting opinions, such stances should be conveyed appropriately.

Anwar said,

“I fully support the menteri besar’s (Aminuddin Harun) move stating that due to the current conditions and uncertainties, it would be best to hold a state election, and Tuanku Muhriz has consented. Even though the federal government is not directly involved (in the issue), we have to give our advice (as) especially for the Malays and the rakyat, the monarchy is not just a name, but (represents) dignity (with) several methods and rules.”

Speaking to reporters after performing Friday prayers in Puchong today, the prime minister affirmed that Putrajaya will continue to defend the dignity and sovereignty of the monarchy.

Anwar emphasised that removing or appointing any royal figure will have serious implications for the nation’s harmony.

1. COURT INJUNCTION

The Seremban High Court’s temporary injunction order TO PRESERVE THE STATUS QUO, as part of a legal battle between the Undang Luak and the state’s Council of the Yang di-Pertuan Besar and the Ruling Chiefs (Dewan Keadilan dan Undang).

2. COMPETING POWERS OF THE CHIEFTAINS( UNDANGS) AND THE STATE RULER (TUAN BESAR)

In a press conference late last night, MB Aminuddin announced the dissolution of the Negeri Sembilan legislature, effective today, AFTER RECEIVING CONSENT  from Tuanku Muhriz.

BUT the chieftains expressed their formal OBJECTION to the state assembly’s dissolution, claiming that their consent was not sought as the state’s “CO-RULERS”. 

They warned on  the validity of the eventual election results, if the dissolution is allowed to proceed.

The chieftains cited several provisions under the state constitution, including Article 28(1), which stipulates that the term “ruler” in the state constitution refers to BOTH  the state Yang di-Pertuan Besar AND the ruling chiefs ( the UNDANGs) “who are available and holding office at the material time”.

3. THE SOURCE OF THE CONFLICT BETWEEN THE CHIEFTAINS AND THE STATE RULER

The problem is a legitimacy dispute: the four Negri Sembilan Undangs claimed they had the customary power to remove the ruler.

But the state government and ruler’s camp say the move to remove the State RULER is INVALID  because one of the Undangs who signed the declaration, Mubarak Dohak of Sungei Ujong, had already been removed from office and therefore lacked authority. 

The confrontation is also about whether the removal process complied with Negeri Sembilan’s CONSTITUTION and Adat Perpatih custom.

The row escalated after the four Undangs met and declared Tuanku Muhriz removed as Yang di-Pertuan Besar, then named Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar as successor. 

That immediately produced a counter-claim from the state government that the declaration had no legal force because Mubarak’s status as Undang had already been revoked.

 The  dispute is not just personal or ceremonial; it goes to the heart of WHO has constitutional authority to choose or dismiss the ruler.

4. THE  LEGAL BATTLE LINE 

At the center of the royal conflict is WHETHER:

- the Undangs acted within their powers, and 

- the required customary procedure was followed. 

The government argued the declaration directly  CONTRADICTED  the state’s constitutional provisions and also critics of the move said the removal of the State Ruler process itself was FLAWED  because the necessary customary participants and procedures were NOT properly involved.

5.IN SUMMARY

This is basically a fight over WHETHER

 a) the chieftains still had the lawful customary authority to depose the ruler, 

OR 

b) the chieftain’s move was invalid because one key Undang had already lost his own office and the procedure was defective.

6. WHAT CONSTITUTIONAL LAW EXPERTS SAY

Negeri Sembilan constitutional experts do not agree that the Undangs’ removal of Tuanku Muhriz was clearly valid. 

Most acknowledge they have the constitutional power to depose a ruler for misconduct or incapacity, BUT  they say the manner in which it was done is LEGALLY QUESTIONABLE  and likely violates due process and customary rules.

6 LEGAL AND CONSTITUTIONAL IMPLICATIONS ACCORDING TO FORMER COURT OF APPEAL JUDGE. HISHAMUDIN YUNUS

Former Court of Appeal Judge Dato’ Seri Hishamudin Yunus has raised serious legal and constitutional concerns about the Undangs’ attempt to remove Tuanku Muhriz as the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan. 

He questions the validity of the proclamation itself, arguing that it is highly doubtful whether any proper due process was carried out in the call for the ruler’s abdication. 

Without a lawful inquiry and established procedure, the proclamation cannot be treated as a legitimate constitutional act.

Hishamudin further points out a critical flaw in the persons involved: the proclamation was read by a former Undang of Sungei Ujong, Datuk Mubarak Dohak, whose own removal from office had already been duly recognised by his own waris and formally validated by the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang. 

This means that the person who delivered the declaration was no longer a legitimate Undang at the time, which severely undermines the legal authority of the proclamation. 

If the signatory lacks the proper status, the entire document cannot be considered valid under the state’s constitutional framework.

He emphasises that any attempt to alter the position of the Ruler must strictly comply with the Laws of the Constitution of Negeri Sembilan 1959 and with established lawful processes. 

The Constitution does NOT  allow arbitrary or informal actions; it requires that removal of a ruler be conducted through clear, formal, and procedural mechanisms that safeguard the integrity of the office. 

In this case, Hishamudin argues that the process appears to have BYPASSED  those requirements.

Finally, Hishamudin states that constitutional order cannot be replaced by unilateral declarations or contested interpretations. 

The stability of the state’s governance depends on adherence to the Constitution and to recognised customary and legal procedures. 

Any attempt to redefine or override those procedures through informal declarations threatens the constitutional foundation of Negeri Sembilan itself. 

His view, therefore, is that the Undangs’ actions, as publicly reported, are constitutionally suspect and likely invalid unless proven to have followed the strict requirements of the state Constitution and Adat Perpatih custom.

7. THE POLITICAL FALLOUT FROM THE ROYAL MESS

Political analysts believe there  is some reason to suspect political motivation by UMNO in this royal crisis but admits there was no evidence that the triggering was politically motivated.

However, what it does show is political opportunism WHEN  all the  UMNO assemblymen in Negeri Sembilan moved against  PKR’s Mentri Besar Aminuddin Harun, said they had lost confidence in his handling of the royal crisis, and that this happened in a state governed by Pakatan Harapan with PKR’s Anwar leading the federal coalition.

And of course,  UMNO president, Zahid Hamidi, appeared to distance himself from the move 
when he said  the UMNO assemblymen as acting on their own.

The timing  of the royal crisis matters: the palace dispute became a state-government crisis, then UMNO withdrew support, and the result was pressure on a PH-led administration. 

What can be safely said is thatlocal UMNO actors exploited or amplified an already volatile royal/customary dispute, while the federal and state leadership tried to manage the fallout.

That makes it look like a mix of royal controversy and power politics, especially because Negeri Sembilan is one of the few states PH controls and losing it would matter politically for Anwar’s coalition.

DON'T ARGUE WITH DONKEYS

"The donkey said to the tiger:
"The grass is blue."

The tiger replied:
"No, the grass is green."

The discussion heated up, and the two decided to go to the lion, the king of the jungle.

Already before reaching the forest, where the lion was sitting on his throne, the donkey began to shout:
"His Highness, is it true that the grass is blue?"

The lion replied:
"True, the grass is blue."

The donkey hurried and continued:
"The tiger disagrees with me and contradicts and annoys me, please punish him."

The king then declared:
"The tiger will be punished with 5 years of silence."

The donkey jumped cheerfully and went on his way, content and repeating:
"The grass is blue!"

The tiger accepted his punishment, but he asked the lion:
"Your Majesty, why have you punished me? After all, the grass is green."

The lion replied:
"In fact, the grass is green."

The tiger asked:
"So why are you punishing me?"

The lion replied:
"That has nothing to do with the question of whether the grass is blue or green. The punishment is because it is not possible for a brave and intelligent creature like you to waste time arguing with a donkey, and on top of that come and bother me with that question."

The worst waste of time is arguing with the fool and fanatic who does not care about truth or reality, but only the victory of his beliefs and illusions. When ignorance screams, intelligence is silent. Your peace and quietness are worth more."

Text:
UPDATE ON THE N9 ROYAL CRISIS  | The Negeri Sembilan Royal Institution Continues to Count Its Last Days 

Many of us do not realise this, but the reason why the Negeri Sembilan State Assembly was dissolved at 11pm on June 4 is because the Undang Yang Empat of Negeri Sembilan were scheduled to meet and install a new Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan on the morning of June 5.

Had the Undang Yang Empat installed Tunku Nadzaruddin as the new Yamtuan Besar, the Negeri Sembilan Menteri Besar Aminuddin Harun would not have been able to dissolve the state assembly with only the permission of the incumbent Yamtuan Besar, Tuanku Muhriz.

He might have had to meet Tunku Nadzaruddin too, to seek the consent of both the feuding claimants to the Yamtuan Besar position, before being able to dissolve the state assembly.

But if Aminuddin met with Tunku Nadzaruddin as well as seek his permission, it would be interpreted as him acknowledging the validity of Tunku Nadzaruddin’s claim to the throne.

It is to avoid this implication, that Aminuddin likely decided at the very last minute—at 11pm on June 4, just hours before the reported installation was to take place—to dissolve the state assembly, although it is likely that he was reluctant to do so.

On the morning of June 5, after considerable brouhaha—which included Tunku Nadzaruddin being prevented by the police from leaving his hotel in Malacca to attend his installation ceremony in Tampin, and two of the Undangs of Negeri Sembilan being prevented from entering the official residence of the Tunku Besar Tampin by the police to convene their meeting—Tunku Nadzaruddin was eventually installed by the Undangs in a hotel in Malacca.

If you search for images of the installation ceremony of Tunku Nadzaruddin, you will likely find him seated on a sofa in a hotel lobby, wearing a relatively ordinary baju melayu, instead of the full royal regalia in yellow.

That image, to me, is a sign of just how farcical the institution of royalty in Negeri Sembilan has become.

Now at this point, you might be cautioning me about being more careful about how I speak about the institution of royalty of Negeri Sembilan, for it might trigger the 3R laws. But at this point, I am not even sure the police would want to take any action against me or anyone, because even they might not be sure about who the Yamtuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan is.

I am not sure I am even “triggering” the 3R laws for regarding the installation ceremony of Tunku Nadzaruddin as farcical, although he was installed by the Undang Yang Empat as the new Yamtuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, when for all intents and purposes, he might just be a regular citizen, on account of his claim to the throne not being fully recognised.

You could even say that criticising Tuanku Muhriz, the incumbent Yamtuan Besar, should not necessarily trigger the 3R laws either, although Tuanku Muhriz is reigning in the Istana Seri Menanti, because technically, he might not be the Yamtuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan either. 

Now If you think that tussle for the throne of Negeri Sembilan, which has left the state with either no kings or two kings or less than one complete king, cannot get any more absurd, hold your horses.

I am more than sure we can expect even more absurdity to occur in the near future.

Just two days ago, as a matter of fact, the Keeper of the Negeri Sembilan ruler’s seal has announced that that although Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Jaafar’s attempt to ascend the throne of Negeri Sembilan is legally invalid, his actions have resulted in him relinquishing his hereditary title of Tunku Panglima Besar of Negeri Sembilan.

That made me wonder.

If an attempt is invalid, does it deserve punishment? If there is punishment, doesn't that signify that the action is of consequence ?And as for the punishment,  how do you remove a hereditary title anyway? By definition, a hereditary title is something you possess by virtue of birth. How do you remove something that a person holds as a birthright?

Titles such as Raja, Tengku, or Tunku are examples of hereditary designations. Can such titles be removed? Can a person of royal lineage be reduced to a commoner through administrative or legal action?

These are some of the questions that are likely playing not only in my mind, but in the minds of all of us who are watching the game of thrones in Negeri Sembilan.

At present, if you were to ask me what the meaning and direction behind the actions of the participants in the Negeri Sembilan royal tussle are, my answer is that it has no meaning - it is only composed of chaos, bewilderment and confusion -  and their actions are leading the institution of royalty in Negeri Sembilan to its demise.

I think those who love and value the institution of royalty in Negeri Sembilan should step in as soon as possible to do whatever it takes to resolve this crisis decisively and that too at the earliest possible time.

It should be resolved decisively, because the crisis is becoming more confusing and bewildering as it progresses, and that is not a good sign, because not only is it a sign of death, it is a sign of a bad death. 

There are two ways a thing dies.

Either it gains peace and clarity as it approaches its end, or it becomes more bewildered and confused as its final moments arrive.

If the former happens, it is a good death.

If the latter happens, it is a bad death.

If the institution of royalty in Negeri Sembilan cannot be saved, then at the very least, those who care for it should ensure that it ends with a good death.

Text:
THE NINE THRONES, THREE TRADITIONS: WHY MALAYSIA POSSESSES ONE OF THE WORLD’S MOST UNUSUAL MONARCHIES

When discussing constitutional monarchies, most people immediately think of Britain, Japan, Thailand, or the Scandinavian kingdoms. In nearly all such systems, succession follows a relatively straightforward principle: the throne passes from parent to child according to a predetermined line of inheritance.

Malaysia, however, chose a different path.

In many ways, the Malaysian monarchy is not a single royal institution but a fascinating collection of several distinct royal traditions that survived colonialism, war, independence, and modern nation-building. The result is arguably one of the most unusual monarchical arrangements anywhere in the world.

The uniqueness lies in the fact that Malaysia accommodates three different methods of royal succession simultaneously: the democratic-elective system of Negeri Sembilan, the rotational hierarchy of Perak, and the hereditary inheritance system practiced by most other Malay states.

⸻

NEGERI SEMBILAN: A MONARCH CHOSEN FROM BELOW

Among all Malay states, Negeri Sembilan stands apart.

Its political culture emerged from the Minangkabau traditions of Sumatra and is heavily influenced by Adat Perpatih, a customary system famous for its matrilineal structure.

The famous proverb:

“Bulat air kerana pembet, bulat manusia kerana muafakat”

captures the spirit of the system perfectly. Consensus matters.

Unlike many monarchies where a prince becomes king simply because he was born first, the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan must be selected by the Undang Yang Empat of Sungai Ujong, Jelebu, Johol, and Rembau.

The process resembles a constitutional electoral college centuries before such terminology became fashionable.

At the grassroots level, clan members choose the Buapak. The Buapak choose the Lembaga. The Lembaga select the Undang. The Undang then choose the Yang di-Pertuan Besar.

One could say that the throne in Negeri Sembilan rests upon layers of consent rather than merely blood.

Trivia:

Negeri Sembilan is often described as possessing one of the few surviving elective monarchies in the world. In practice, a prince may possess impeccable royal ancestry and yet never become ruler if he lacks the confidence of the Undang.

⸻

PERAK: THE ROYAL WAITING ROOM

If Negeri Sembilan resembles an electoral monarchy, Perak resembles a carefully managed promotion ladder.

The Perak succession system developed after centuries of royal experience, including succession disputes that occasionally led to conflict.

Rather than relying solely on primogeniture, Perak created a structured hierarchy of titled princes known as the Raja-Raja Bergelar.

A prince typically progresses through a sequence of positions:

* Raja Kecil Bongsu
* Raja Kecil Tengah
* Raja Kecil Sulung
* Raja Kecil Besar
* Raja Di Hilir
* Raja Muda

Only after reaching Raja Muda may he eventually become Sultan.

The system resembles a civil service promotion scheme, except the ultimate office happens to be the throne itself.

Importantly, advancement is not entirely automatic. The state’s royal council considers factors such as conduct, health, capability, and suitability.

Trivia:

Historians often note that Perak’s system is one of the most sophisticated royal succession mechanisms in Southeast Asia. It allows multiple branches of the royal family to remain relevant rather than concentrating all future succession in a single household.

⸻

THE TEMENGGUNG STATES: THE FAMILIAR ROYAL MODEL

Most Malaysians are more familiar with the third system.

States such as Johor, Selangor, Pahang, Kedah, Kelantan, Terengganu, and Perlis generally follow principles influenced by Adat Temenggung.

This model is straightforward.

The throne passes from father to son through the male line. The designated heir is known early in life and typically carries titles such as Tengku Mahkota, Raja Muda, or Tuanku Syed Putra’s equivalent successor title.

When the ruler dies or abdicates, succession occurs with minimal uncertainty.

The principal advantage is stability.

Everyone already knows who the next ruler will be.

Trivia:

This is the succession model most commonly found throughout the world’s monarchies, from Europe to the Middle East and Asia. It is often considered the easiest system for ensuring continuity and avoiding disputes.

⸻

A MONARCHY OF EXTRAORDINARY DIVERSITY

What makes Malaysia remarkable is not merely that these three systems exist.

It is that they exist side by side within one federation.

An elected ruler in Negeri Sembilan, a rotational succession system in Perak, and hereditary monarchies elsewhere all coexist under the same constitutional framework.

The story becomes even more extraordinary when one remembers that the Yang di-Pertuan Agong himself is selected through a rotational arrangement among the nine Malay rulers—a practice virtually unique in the modern world.

Few nations can claim to possess an elected monarch, a rotational monarchy, hereditary monarchies, and a rotating federal kingship simultaneously.

Malaysia can.

And perhaps that is one of the country’s most overlooked historical achievements: a constitutional system that transformed centuries of diverse Malay customs into a functioning modern federation without erasing the uniqueness of any of them.

The result is a monarchy that is not merely inherited. It is also negotiated, rotated, elected, and preserved—a living museum of Malay political history still operating in the twenty-first century.
To maintain the system, it's really costly. As long as it brings stability, the system maintains. But when the system becomes messy and messier, the next generation may abandon it one day.

Text:
This is my personal opinion based on my understanding of the Constitution of Negeri Sembilan, Adat Perpatih, and the events that have been reported. I welcome correction from those who are more knowledgeable on the subject.

Negeri Sembilan has one of the most unique constitutional monarchies in the world.

Unlike the hereditary monarchies found in most other Malay states, the Yang diPertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan is elected. The institution traces its roots to the Minangkabau tradition and Adat Perpatih, a customary system that differs significantly from the Adat Temenggong practised in most other Malay states.

Under the Constitution of Negeri Sembilan, the Yang diPertuan Besar is elected by the Undang Yang Empat of Sungai Ujong, Jelebu, Johol and Rembau. These four Undangs are not merely ceremonial figures. They occupy a central role within the constitutional and customary structure of the state and are entrusted with the responsibility of selecting the Ruler.

(Alongside the Undang Yang Empat stands the Tunku Besar of Tampin, who occupies a unique and respected position within Negeri Sembilan's traditional hierarchy. 

Although the Tunku Besar does not participate in the formal election of the Yang diPertuan Besar, Tampin remains an important component of the state's adat structure and has historically been regarded as part of the broader ruling establishment of Negeri Sembilan.)

This means succession is not automatic.

Unlike other royal houses where the throne often passes to the eldest son, the Undangs retain the authority to determine who among the eligible Putera Yang Empat, is most suitable to ascend the throne. While the sons of a reigning or deceased Yang diPertuan Besar may be considered first, the Undangs are not bound to choose the eldest son if they believe another candidate is more suitable according to the Constitution and adat.

History demonstrates this clearly. When Tuanku Munawir ibni Tuanku Abdul Rahman passed away in 1967, his son, Tuanku Muhriz, was not selected. Instead, the Undangs elected another of Tuanku Abdul Rahman's son, Tuanku Jaafar ibni Tuanku Abdul Rahman as the Yang diPertuan Besar. Later, upon the passing of Tuanku Jaafar in 2008, the Undangs elected Tuanku Muhriz and not the popular and charming Tunku Naquiyuddin ibni Tuanku Jaafar. This illustrates that the Negeri Sembilan system is not based on automatic inheritance but rather on selection by the Undangs. The powerful Undangs.

Now the Undangs themselves derive their legitimacy from the Adat Perpatih system. Their selection is rooted in customary processes that have existed for generations. Traditionally, acceptance by the adat institutions and adherence to custom have always been important considerations.

In my view, the present crisis did not begin with the question of who should become the next Yang diPertuan Besar. Rather, it appears to have begun with the controversy involving the Undang of Sungai Ujong, who reportedly faced numerous allegations and was subsequently removed from office.

Whether that removal was justified or not is a matter of debate. However, from the perspective of natural justice, I believe that any person facing serious allegations should be afforded a meaningful opportunity to answer the charges against him before a decision is made. This is important. Allegations appeared of his impropriety. 

The dispute then appears to have expanded into a broader disagreement concerning the powers of the Undangs, the role of the Yang diPertuan Besar, the position of the Tunku Besar of Tampin, and questions relating to succession.

It is important to remember that under Negeri Sembilan's unique constitutional framework, no Yang diPertuan Besar can simply appoint his own successor. The power to elect the Yang diPertuan Besar rests with the Undang Yang Empat. That is the very foundation of the Negeri Sembilan system and what distinguishes it from other Malay monarchies.

It is from this foundational principle of Undang supremacy that the legitimacy of Tunku Nadzaruddin as the 12th Yang diPertuan Besar emerges. On April 19, the Undang Yang Empat, acting within their customary sovereign capacity as the absolute electors of the state, exercised their ancient authority to declare the removal of Tuanku Muhriz and subsequently named Tunku Nadzaruddin as his rightful successor. 

While detractors point to the June 5 proclamation ceremony taking place in Alor Gajah, Melaka, rather than within state borders, this geographical shift was a direct consequence of outside administrative interference that blocked the Undangs from convening at the official residence of the Tunku Besar of Tampin. A physical venue change, forced by external pressures, does not diminish the constitutional weight of a unanimous decision made by the Undangs themselves.

To reject Tunku Nadzaruddin's ascension is to fundamentally misunderstand the core of Negeri Sembilan’s unique constitutional framework. If the Yang diPertuan Besar is an elected monarch, his legitimacy flows entirely from the trust of his electors, the Undang Yang Empat. When the Undangs collectively determine that a shift in leadership is necessary for the preservation of Adat Perpatih, their decree must be respected as the highest customary law of the  land. Therefore, despite the pushback from the state palace administration and federal figures, Tunku Nadzaruddin’s appointment stands as a lawful manifestation of Adat supremacy, demonstrating that the throne of Negeri Sembilan belongs to the custom, not to a single hereditary line.

The various claims and counterclaims that have emerged regarding succession, abdication, appointments and removals should therefore, in my opinion, be examined carefully against both the Constitution and the customs of Adat Perpatih.

Equally, if allegations have been made against any party, whether involving the royal institution, the Undangs or other adat authorities, those allegations should be addressed through a process that respects fairness and natural justice. Every person accused of wrongdoing should have the opportunity to respond before judgment is passed, including the Undangs as well as the Yang DiPertuan Besar.

Ultimately, I believe this dispute is larger than any individual. It concerns the balance of authority between the Yang diPertuan Besar, the Undang Yang Empat and the traditional institutions of Negeri Sembilan, including Tampin, as well as the continued preservation of Negeri Sembilan's unique constitutional and adat heritage.

Only a transparent process, grounded in the Constitution, Adat Perpatih and the principles of natural justice, will allow the people of Negeri Sembilan to determine where legitimacy truly lies.

Inappropriate to 'remove' the sitting State Ruler, Tuanku Muhriz, without clear reason, says Former Law Minister  Datuk Zaid Ibrahim

PETALING JAYA:

https://www.facebook.com/share/r/1KQAUmeRWE/?mibextid=wwXIfr

 Former law minister Zaid Ibrahim has described the reported "removal" of Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan as inappropriate, saying no clear misconduct was ever put before the public to justify the move.

Zaid said the central question was not merely whether the undangs have the power to appoint or remove a ruler, but whether that power is exercised fairly and reasonably.

He said the Negeri Sembilan constitution allows for the removal of a ruler in cases of serious misconduct or dereliction of duty.

"But we, the public, have not been told what wrongdoing Tuanku Muhriz supposedly committed. We simply do not know," he said on the latest episode of his podcast.

"Therefore, even if the four undangs have the constitutional power to remove Tuanku Muhriz, I do not think it is appropriate. It is disproportionate.

"I believe the spirit of the constitutional provisions has been set aside. Even if the power to remove him exists, I do not think it should have been exercised in this manner."

His remarks come after the four undangs reportedly proclaimed Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja'afar as the 12th Yang di-Pertuan Besarat a ceremony held at a hotel in Melaka.

It is understood that the proclamation was made by the Jelebu undang, Maarof Mat Rashad, on behalf of the four chieftains.

The four undangs had first announced Tuanku Muhriz's  “dismissal" on April 19. Tuanku Muhriz was installed as the 11th Yang di-Pertuan Besar at Istana Besar Seri Menanti on Oct 26, 2009, following the death of Tuanku Ja'afar Tuanku Abdul Rahman.

  The Seremban High Court had earlier on the same day issued a temporary injunction restraining the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang from meeting or making decisions, and barring it from removing its secretary, Raja Norazli Raja Nordin.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has said that Tuanku Muhriz remains the legitimate ruler of Negeri Sembilan, adding that the matter must be resolved through proper channels.

Text:
TWO THRONES ONE ELECTION
The Crisis That an Election Cannot Solve
Betty Teh | Constituition 

To understand the constitutional crisis that has brought Negeri Sembilan to a simultaneous state election and royal succession dispute, you have to start not on April 19 when four Undang declared the ruler deposed but nearly a year earlier when the seeds of the confrontation were planted. On May 13 2025, Mubarak Dohak, the Undang of Sungai Ujong and the most senior of the four territorial chiefs who hold the power to elect and remove Negeri Sembilan's ruler — was stripped of his title as Datuk Klana Petra following 33 alleged violations of customary and Islamic laws. The decision was made at a meeting of the Telaga Undang, the matriarchal clan leaders and heirs of Sungai Ujong. He was removed not by the ruler. He was removed by his own customary structure.

Mubarak disputed this and refused to vacate. For nearly a year the dispute simmered within Sungai Ujong's customary institutions. Then on April 17 2026, the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang — the council chaired by Tuanku Muhriz held a special session at Istana Besar Seri Menanti. The DKU was presented with the 33 reasons for Mubarak's removal and advised the Luak of Sungai Ujong to formally accept it. Tuanku Muhriz, as chair of the DKU, presided over and accepted that advice. The removal was formalised. Mubarak Dohak was no longer the Undang of Sungai Ujong. Sinar Daily

Two days later Mubarak struck back.

On April 19, Mubarak appeared at the Balai Undang Luak Sungai Ujong alongside three other Undang — Maarof Mat Rashad of Jelebu, Muhammed Abdullah of Johol and Abdul Rahim Yasin of Rembau and read a declaration deposing Tuanku Muhriz as Yang di Pertuan Besar. No specific reasons were given. No full enquiry had been conducted. The declaration was announced at a press conference and streamed on Facebook. 

The same man whose removal had just been formalised by the DKU two days earlier was now using his claimed authority as Undang to depose the ruler who had just accepted that removal. 

The state government rejected the declaration immediately. Aminuddin declared it void on the most basic of grounds — Mubarak had been removed from office with effect from May 13 2025 and had no authority to sign or read any declaration as Undang. 

But the other three Undang disputed this entirely. They issued a statement saying the DKU on April 17 had not made a collective and unanimous decision on Mubarak's removal, calling Aminuddin's account untrue and not in accordance with the Negeri Sembilan constitution. They also declared that Aminuddin was no longer fit to lead the state administration and should be replaced. 

Two versions of what happened in the same DKU meeting on April 17. The government's version — Mubarak was validly removed. The Undang's version — no such unanimous decision was made. The minutes of that meeting became so contested that the three Undang and Mubarak filed an originating summons in the Seremban High Court seeking a copy of the DKU meeting minutes. 

This is the origin of everything that followed. Not a sudden eruption after 18 years of stable rule. A confrontation that had been building since May 2025 when Mubarak lost his title within his own customary structure and which detonated on April 19 when he chose the most dramatic available instrument of retaliation: the constitutional power to depose a ruler.

To understand why that power exists and why it created such a crisis when invoked, you have to understand what makes Negeri Sembilan constitutionally unique. Every other Malay state has a hereditary monarchy — the throne passes from father to son, predetermined by bloodline. Negeri Sembilan has never done this. Under the Adat Perpatih system, a matrilineal customary law tradition established in 1773 and derived from the Minangkabau people of West Sumatra — the Yang di Pertuan Besar is elected by four territorial chiefs known as the Undang Yang Empat. The Undang of Sungai Ujong, Rembau, Jelebu and Johol collectively hold the power to install the ruler. 

Under Article 10 of the written Negeri Sembilan state constitution which codified the adat — they also hold the power to remove him under four specified conditions: insanity, stupidity, acts that disgrace Islam, or acts that disgrace the royal institution. But crucially the constitution requires a full and complete enquiry before any such removal. No enquiry was held on April 19. The declaration was made without one.

The legal problem with the April 19 declaration therefore has two independent bases. Former judge Hishamudin said it was invalid first because Mubarak who signed and read it had already been removed as Undang and had no authority to act. And second because no full enquiry had been conducted as required by Article X of the state constitution. Either ground alone was sufficient to make the declaration void. Together they made it constitutionally indefensible. 

Yet the three remaining Undang stood by it. And they had their own legal strategist in the form of Tan Sri Rais Yatim, former law minister, Negeri Sembilan native, and the public voice of the traditionalist faction — who argued that all adat procedures had been properly followed. 

Two lawyers. Two readings of the same constitutional text. Both citing the same articles. Neither willing to concede.

The crisis did not stay within the palace. Four days after the April 19 declaration, the Negeri Sembilan State Legislative Assembly was scheduled to open its first meeting of the fourth session, a routine constitutionally required sitting that must occur at least once every six months. The Undang issued a statement the night before demanding postponement until all customary transfer of power processes were completed. Tuanku Muhriz arrived anyway. His arrival at Wisma Negeri on April 23 accompanied by his consort, his inspection of the guard of honour, and his delivery of the royal address was the first time in his entire reign since 2008 that the four Undang had not attended a state assembly opening. 

All 36 assemblymen were present except one on official duty. The Speaker adjourned the sitting immediately after the royal address, saying he hoped the dispute could be clarified before the next sitting. The assembly opened and adjourned on the same day. 

The royal crisis then consumed the political one. Fourteen UMNO state assemblymen withdrew their support from Menteri Besar Aminuddin citing his perceived alignment with Tuanku Muhriz against the Undang. PH fell to seventeen seats in a thirty six seat assembly, two short of a majority. 

The government that had defended the constitution's position on the ruler's legitimacy was now itself rendered constitutionally uncertain. The two crises fed each other. Aminuddin's defence of Tuanku Muhriz's legitimacy became the grounds for his own government's delegitimisation. The UMNO assemblymen who chose the Undang over the constitution had effectively handed the traditionalist faction a second instrument of pressure — the assembly numbers.

Then June 5 produced its extraordinary scenes. On the same day Aminuddin dissolved the assembly with Tuanku Muhriz's consent, police blocked the Undang from entering the venue for their planned DKU meeting in Tampin. The High Court issued an interim injunction halting proceedings. The Undang relocated to a hotel in Alor Gajah in Melaka, a different state entirely and there proclaimed Tunku Nadzaruddin as Yang di Pertuan Besar for the second time. 

Anwar reaffirmed Tuanku Muhriz as the legitimate ruler and questioned the dignity of a royal proclamation conducted in a hotel. 

Two men now claim the throne. One recognised by the federal government, the state government, and the courts. One recognised by the four chiefs who have held the constitutional power to elect rulers since 1773. 

And an election has been called to resolve a political crisis that the dissolution itself cannot resolve — because the deeper constitutional question of who is the legitimate Yang di Pertuan Besar will outlast any electoral result.

If PH wins and Aminuddin returns as MB he will continue recognising Tuanku Muhriz. If BN wins a new MB must decide before whom he takes his oath. Which ruler signs the instruments of government. Which ruler's consent is required for future dissolutions. The election produces a government. It does not produce an answer.

What makes this crisis genuinely unprecedented is not its complexity but its location. It lives in the gap between two legal systems that have coexisted in Negeri Sembilan for 253 years — the written constitution and the unwritten adat. The written constitution codified the adat but did not resolve what happens when they contradict each other. 

For 253 years that contradiction never fully surfaced. It surfaced on May 13 2025 when Mubarak Dohak lost his title. It detonated on April 19 2026 when he used the most powerful instrument available to him to strike back. And it has not been resolved by courts, injunctions, proclamations in hotel ballrooms, or the dissolution of a state assembly. 

Sixty days of campaigning will not resolve it either.
Another layer to the N9 palace intrigue.

Text:
Malaysia’s Conference of Rulers postponed over NS ruler’s legitimacy

Issue now potentially could undermine the stability of the monarchy

As the prime minister Anwar Ibrahim calls on royalty to be left out of politics, there is some community concerns over a number of Royal decrees, and the DAP’s Tony Pua has raised questions about royal roles in politics and the role of the Sedition Act.
It is now during this time that the Conference of Rulers has been postponed at short notice amid an ongoing dispute over the throne of Negeri Sembilan, underscoring the paramount importance of preserving the stability and unity of the constitutional monarchy.
The rare cancellation of the meeting, originally scheduled for June 23 to 25, reflects the deep concern among the nine rulers over the unfolding crisis in Negeri Sembilan. Such postponements are highly uncommon. The last occurring during the Covid-19 lockdowns in 2021. This highlights how seriously the institution views any threat to the established order and harmony within the royal houses.
At the heart of the matter are competing claims to the position of Yang di-Pertuan Besar. The state and federal governments continue to recognise Tuanku Muhriz Munawir as the rightful ruler. However, the four Undang (territorial chieftains) have moved to install his nephew, Tunku Nadzaruddin Ja’afar, prompting a complex legal and customary dispute. This uncertainty has already triggered the dissolution of the state legislative assembly on June 5, raising questions about the feasibility and appropriateness of proceeding with state elections on August 1.
The Conference of Rulers serves as a vital pillar of Malaysia’s constitutional framework, providing a forum for the monarchs to deliberate on matters of national importance, including those affecting Malay customs, Islam, and constitutional amendments. Any perception of division or unresolved conflict within this esteemed body risks eroding public confidence in the monarchy’s stabilizing role. In a diverse nation like Malaysia, the monarchy’s continuity and impartial dignity are essential safeguards for national unity and social harmony.
Background rooted in Adat Perpatih
Under Negeri Sembilan’s unique Adat Perpatih customs, the Undang hold traditional authority to elect and, in exceptional cases following due inquiry, remove a ruler. Tensions reportedly escalated after disagreements over privileges and a decision by Tuanku Muhriz regarding the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU). The subsequent sequence of events, including the Undang’s removal ceremony on April 19, the state government’s late-night announcement of dissolution, and the attempted installation of the new claimant have all created a delicate situation now before the courts.
Interim court injunctions have been issued, and the matter is slated for further hearings in July. Both sides have acted within what they view as their legitimate roles, yet the priority must now be a clear, orderly, and legally sound resolution that upholds the dignity of the institution and respects established conventions. Prolonged uncertainty serves no one and could inadvertently politicize an institution that should remain above partisan contention.
Broader implications for stability
The dispute has already had political repercussions, including shifts in support within the state assembly and implications for Pakatan Harapan (PH) ahead of the polls. A further erosion of institutional clarity could complicate governance and public trust at a time when political stability is already under pressure from other state elections, such as the upcoming one in Johor.
Malaysia’s monarchy has long been a symbol of continuity and a moderating force in the nation’s federal democracy. The rulers’ decision to pause the conference demonstrates prudent leadership and a collective commitment to safeguarding the monarchy’s integrity rather than allowing rushed proceedings that might deepen divisions. A swift and amicable resolution, ideally through dialogue, respect for custom, and judicial clarity is in the best interest of Negeri Sembilan and the federation as a whole.
The next scheduled Conference of Rulers in October will offer an important opportunity to reaffirm unity. In the interim, all parties are urged to exercise restraint, prioritize legal channels, and place the long-term stability and reverence of the royal institution above all other considerations. The strength of Malaysia’s constitutional monarchy lies in its enduring role as a unifying pillar, a role that must be protected with care.

Text:
THE THRONE, THE UNDANG, AND THE DAY ADAT STARTED ARGUING WITH ITSELF

There are few things Malaysians assume will remain stable forever.

The sunrise.

The price of nasi lemak eventually going up.

Traffic jams appearing from nowhere.

And royal succession.

The first three occasionally surprise us.

The fourth is not supposed to.

Which is why the recent turmoil surrounding Negeri Sembilan has left many Malaysians staring at their phones the way one stares at a GPS that suddenly announces:

“Please drive into the lake.”

Because for a brief moment, it seemed as though an ancient institution built on centuries of custom had wandered into a constitutional maze while carrying several competing maps.

And nobody appeared entirely certain which map was the official one.

⸻

THE STATE WHERE DEMOCRACY’S OLDER COUSIN STILL LIVES

Most Malaysians understand monarchy through a simple formula.

King dies.

Prince succeeds.

People shout “Daulat Tuanku.”

Lunch is served.

Negeri Sembilan, however, has always been the intellectual in the family.

The cousin who insists on explaining the rules before playing the game.

Its royal system is not built upon simple inheritance.

It is built upon Adat Perpatih.

Consensus.

Selection.

Customary authority.

Institutional layers.

Historical legitimacy.

In other words, Negeri Sembilan’s political architecture resembles a beautifully handcrafted antique clock.

Elegant.

Unique.

Sophisticated.

And occasionally so complicated that nobody remembers which gear moves which hand.

⸻

WHEN EVERYONE CLAIMS TO BE THE REAL REFEREE

The problem with legitimacy is that it functions much like Wi-Fi.

Nobody notices it when it works.

Everybody notices it when it doesn’t.

In ordinary times, the authority of an Undang appears settled.

The authority of the Yang di-Pertuan Besar appears settled.

The authority of customary institutions appears settled.

Then suddenly competing groups emerge.

Each side cites custom.

Each side cites law.

Each side cites history.

Each side cites procedure.

Each side insists it is defending tradition.

And the ordinary rakyat begins feeling like a spectator watching two lawyers argue over ownership of the same house while the house itself is still occupied.

The result is not clarity.

The result is confusion wearing ceremonial attire.

⸻

ADAT: THE WORLD’S OLDEST OPERATING SYSTEM

There is a curious habit among Malaysians.

Whenever custom is discussed, people split into two tribes.

The first tribe treats adat as sacred software.

Never update.

Never modify.

Never question.

The second tribe treats adat as an old Nokia phone.

Interesting historically.

Not especially useful today.

Both positions miss something important.

Custom survives because it adapts.

Otherwise every civilisation would still be travelling by buffalo cart and communicating through smoke signals.

The irony is that traditions which survive centuries are usually the traditions most capable of evolving.

The traditions that refuse all adaptation eventually become museum exhibits.

Beautiful.

Respected.

And largely irrelevant to daily life.

⸻

THE RESORT, THE PROCLAMATION, AND THE NATIONAL DOUBLE TAKE

Politics occasionally produces strange optics.

This episode produced extraordinary optics.

A proclamation.

A royal dispute.

A competing narrative.

And a location that generated almost as much discussion as the proclamation itself.

The entire affair felt less like a carefully choreographed constitutional process and more like a historical drama whose script had accidentally escaped into social media before the final edit.

For ordinary Malaysians unfamiliar with Negeri Sembilan’s constitutional intricacies, the spectacle raised obvious questions.

If a proclamation can be made publicly, who has authority?

If authority is disputed, who decides?

If everyone claims legitimacy, where does legitimacy actually reside?

These are not merely legal questions.

They are existential questions for any institution.

⸻

WHEN CUSTOM MEETS FACEBOOK

In previous centuries, customary disputes remained largely within customary circles.

Village leaders discussed them.

Traditional authorities resolved them.

The wider public heard about them months later, if at all.

Today?

A disagreement can become a livestream.

A proclamation can become a TikTok clip.

A constitutional argument can become a WhatsApp forward before breakfast.

Custom moves at the speed of tradition.

Social media moves at the speed of caffeine.

The collision is inevitable.

And institutions built for patience suddenly find themselves being judged by audiences demanding answers before lunchtime.

⸻

“BIAR MATI ANAK, JANGAN MATI ADAT” — REALLY?

Perhaps the most fascinating aspect of the debate is how often Malaysians invoke the famous proverb:

“Biar mati anak, jangan mati adat.”

People quote it with such confidence one might assume they have personally tested the policy.

Let us be honest.

Nobody chooses tradition over their child.

Nobody.

Not the loudest defender of custom.

Not the fiercest guardian of heritage.

Not the uncle giving lectures at weddings.

The proverb was never meant to be taken literally.

It was meant to emphasise the importance of social order.

But somewhere along the way, some people began treating it as though customs exist for their own sake rather than for the wellbeing of the community they are supposed to serve.

That is like preserving the steering wheel while forgetting the purpose of the car.

⸻

THE REAL CRISIS IS NOT THE THRONE

The deepest issue may not be who occupies the throne.

Nor who signs which proclamation.

Nor which faction claims legitimacy.

The deeper issue is public confidence.

Institutions survive not only through legal authority.

They survive through belief.

The moment ordinary people begin asking:

“Who is actually in charge?”

an institution has entered dangerous territory.

Because authority depends on recognition.

And recognition depends on trust.

⸻

CONCLUSION: WHEN THE ROOTS ARGUE, THE TREE SHAKES

Negeri Sembilan’s unique system has survived wars, colonialism, independence, modernisation, and globalisation.

That alone deserves respect.

But every living institution eventually encounters the same challenge.

How does it preserve tradition while maintaining legitimacy in a modern world?

How does it honour history without becoming trapped by it?

How does it ensure that custom remains a source of stability rather than confusion?

Because ultimately, the strength of a throne does not come from wood, gold, titles, or ceremonies.

It comes from confidence.

And confidence, unlike custom, cannot be inherited.

It must be renewed.

Again and again.

Wallahua’lam.

When branches argue, leaves tremble.

But when roots argue, the entire tree begins to wonder where it stands.

KUALA PILAH, June 25 —The Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, has consented to hold the royal audience ceremony to formalise the installation of the Undang of Luak Rembau at Istana Besar Seri Menanti this Saturday.

The royal decree was conveyed by Tunku Besar Seri Menanti, Tunku Ali Redhauddin Tuanku Muhriz, during an audience with the Datuk-Datuk Adat of Rembau at Istana Besar Seri Menanti today.

“I am informed that the selection of the 22nd Undang of Rembau was conducted in accordance with the adat (customs) and traditions practised in Rembau.

“I wish to convey the consent of my father, Tuanku Muhriz, for the Istiadat Menghadap Menjunjung Duli Bagi Menyempurnakan Kejadian Undang Luak Rembau. For matters relating to the ceremony and preparations, the adat leaders may discuss them with the Orang Empat Istana. I pray that all arrangements proceed smoothly,” he said.

Meanwhile, chairman of the Kerapatan Buapak Delapan ceremony for the Biduanda Nan Dua Carak customary clan, Datuk Juan Datuk Zulkipli Shamsudin, said Hassan Ab Hamid, 67, had been selected as the 22nd Undang of Rembau in accordance with established adat procedures.

Zulkipli stressed that under the Adat Perpatih system, an Undang is not appointed by the Yang Dipertuan Besar but is chosen through the customary processes of the luak itself.

“The role of His Royal Highness is to receive representatives of the luak when they seek an audience and, when required by custom, to grant consent and recognition to the decision reached by the community.

“His Royal Highness does not summon, choose or appoint any individual at his own discretion. Any statement suggesting otherwise reflects a misunderstanding of the adat that have governed Negeri Sembilan for centuries,” he said.

The previous Undang of Rembau, Datuk Lela Maharaja Datuk Muhamad Sharip Othman, died of old age on May 15, 2024, at the age of 83. — Bernama
